description: We are a team consisting of members from Uganda dedicated to building a web application showing the variation of burning activity over time. We have skills in Web design and 3D animation.
summary:
The Burner’s Archive is an interactive web application that turns two decades of satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar. MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) records can’t be compared directly, so we apply a Kernel Density Estimation model that reconciles them into a single baseline from 2000 to today.

Users search any city or country, or draw their own area, on a 3D globe and switch between Joint (both satellites merged), MODIS only and VIIRS only to see what each sensor misses. Fires are colour-coded: red for live, amber for suspected, violet for recent past. Users can add notes to any spot, and an alert shows the nearest active fire to them. The Burning Calendar shows fires day by day, or as a month-by-month heatmap with downloads, and Insights explains how the two sensors differ and how we merge them. Spark, our guide mascot, walks first-time users through it.

This gives emergency responders, scientists and land managers a trustworthy fire history for any area, so they can spot seasonal patterns and unusual activity, and prepare for critical periods as fire seasons intensify.
details:
The Burner’s Archive turns two decades of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar. MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) records can’t be compared directly, so a Python pipeline applies a Kernel Density Estimation model that reconciles them into a single baseline from 2000 to today. A Node.js and Express API serves the processed series to our React front end.

Users search any city or country, or draw their own area, on a 3D CesiumJS globe. A three-way switch shows Joint (both satellites merged), MODIS only or VIIRS only. Fires are colour-coded: red for live, amber for suspected, violet for recent past, and tapping a spot shows details and lets the user add notes. The Burning Calendar shows fires day by day, or as a month-by-month heatmap with downloads. A Country Footprints page plots burning activity for different countries from 2000 to 2025, so patterns can be compared quickly. A comparison game lets users compare countries or cities against each other. Insights explains how the sensors differ and how we merge them, and a Methodology page lets anyone walk through our entire pipeline and an alert shows the nearest active fire to the user.

Benefits

Users get one trustworthy record instead of two incompatible ones. They can see which months and years burn most, compare current activity with history, and check what each satellite misses. The country plots and comparison game make it easy to put one place’s fire activity in context against another’s, without needing data skills.

Intended impact

We want early-warning teams, emergency responders, scientists and land managers to anticipate critical fire periods, guide monitoring and respond faster as fire weather intensifies. MODIS is nearing the end of its life, so a harmonized baseline keeps decades of history usable as VIIRS takes over. Because the full pipeline is open to explore, others can check, trust and build on the method.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA Earthdata FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspots; our supporting analysis of the full historical dataset was processed on Kaggle.
  • Pipeline: Python (pandas, geopandas, czml3).
  • Back end: Node.js and Express.
  • Front end: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, CesiumJS through resium.
  • Hosting and workflow: Firebase Hosting, GitHub and GitHub Codespaces. No special hardware was needed.

What is creative about it

  • Spark, a flame mascot, guides first-time users through a 9-step interactive tour, so a 3D globe and a technical data story stay approachable.
  • Users can see the harmonization instead of trusting it, by switching between Joint, MODIS and VIIRS views.
  • Fire history appears both on a 3D globe and as a calendar heatmap, so a viewer can spot seasonality at a glance.

Factors the team considered

  • Sensor differences: resolution, sensitivity and observation schedule.
  • Audience: emergency managers need quick, readable views and clear baselines.
  • Usability: a guided tour, simple switches and downloads for people who aren’t data specialists.
  • Data size: the raw data is huge about 45GB, so only processed summaries are served to the site.
  • Team: These members are from Uganda, with web design and 3D animation skills, shaped the visual approach.
